Maladaptive Strategies.value: Being reminded of the event by others
I release my tension with sexual fantasies/ activities
Being around people in authority or uniform

Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together

Negative Appraisals.value: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
I have to be on guard all the time

vignette: Leila's eyes scan the room before she even notices the decor. It's a habit she's developed over the past year, ever since that night when her sense of safety was shattered. She can't remember exactly how many months it's been – time feels distorted, and memories blend together in a jumbled mess. What she does recall is the feeling of being trapped, of having no control over what was happening to her. It started with the sound of sirens outside her apartment building. Leila had always associated ambulances with helping people, but now the wail of their horns sends her heart racing. She'll often find herself frozen in fear, unable to move or breathe until the noise fades away. Her husband, Raj, has tried to reassure her that everything will be okay, but even his calm demeanor can't shake off the feeling of impending doom. Leila avoids talking about the assault with anyone, including Raj. She's convinced that if she thinks about it too much, she'll lose her grip on reality. Her mind is already a jumble of fragmented memories – the taste of her attacker's skin, the feel of his weight on top of her, the sound of her own screams echoing in her head. These disjointed pieces haunt her, refusing to coalesce into a coherent narrative. At work, Leila finds herself constantly scanning for exits. She'll sit near the door during meetings, just in case she needs to make a quick escape. Her colleagues have started to notice her agitation, but they attribute it to stress from the demanding call center job. What they don't know is that Leila's hypervigilance extends far beyond the office walls. She's always on the lookout for potential dangers – suspicious strangers lurking in alleys, unattended bags on public transportation, or even just an unexpected movement nearby. One thing that brings Leila temporary relief from her anxiety is sex. She'll often initiate intimacy with Raj as a way to release tension and distract herself from her thoughts. It's not about pleasure; it's about coping. Yet, this coping mechanism has started to take a toll on their relationship. Raj feels like he's being used, rather than being a source of comfort. Leila avoids authority figures whenever possible – police officers, doctors, even security guards at the mall. She can't explain why, but there's something about uniforms that makes her skin crawl. When she sees happy families on social media or in public, it triggers a deep sense of inadequacy within her. Why couldn't she have had a normal childhood, free from trauma? Why did this have to happen to her? The weight of these emotions has become overwhelming. Leila's relationships are suffering – Raj feels helpless, and her friends are starting to drift away. She's constantly exhausted from being on high alert all the time. Recently, Leila realized she couldn't keep going like this. The fear, the anxiety, the shame – it was suffocating her. That's when she finally decided to seek help. As she sits in the therapist's office, Leila is most afraid of facing the memories she's tried so hard to suppress. She hopes that someday she'll be able to break free from this prison of fear and find a sense of peace again.
